title: Maximum Subarray
description: Brute force to optimized: summing from every starting index versus Kadane's single running "best ending here" recurrence.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous, non-empty subarray with the largest sum, and return that sum.

blocks.caption: At each position, decide to extend the running subarray or restart fresh, whichever gives a bigger sum

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums, possibly containing negative numbers, find the largest possible sum achievable by any contiguous, non-empty subarray.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Hiker Tracking Net Elevation Gain
blocks.text: Like a hiker tracking net elevation change along a trail with both uphill and downhill stretches, wanting to know the best possible net gain over any single continuous stretch of the hike. If the net change so far has gone negative, it's never worth carrying that deficit forward. It's always better to start measuring fresh from the current point, since a negative starting balance can only make every future stretch look worse than it truly is.

blocks.caption: A negative running sum is discarded by restarting fresh, since it can only hurt what follows

blocks.text: Edge case: nums has only one element
When nums has exactly one element, that single element is the only possible non-empty subarray, so it is trivially the answer, regardless of its sign.
Before checking every possible subarray's sum directly, notice that at any given position, only one running decision ever matters: keep extending, or start over.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For any ending position, the best subarray ending exactly there either extends the best subarray ending at the previous position, or starts fresh at the current position alone.

Observation 2: If the best running sum ending at the previous position is negative, carrying it forward can only make the current position's sum worse than the current element by itself.

Observation 3: So the recurrence is simply: current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]), always keeping the better of "extend" versus "restart here".

Observation 4: Track the overall best sum seen across every position's "current" value throughout a single linear pass.

Recognizing that only the immediately preceding running sum matters (not the entire history) is what collapses an apparently expensive all-subarrays search into a single O(1)-per-element decision.
This is the classic Kadane's Algorithm pattern: maintain a running "best sum ending here" value, discarding it and restarting whenever it would only hurt what comes next.
For every possible starting index, extend forward one element at a time, tracking the running sum directly.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, accumulating a running sum.
Compare every intermediate running sum against the best found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh running sum is used for every starting position, since each independent walk accumulates its own subarray sum.
best is compared against every intermediate sum, not just the final one, since the maximum for a given start could occur partway through.
best is initialized to nums[0] rather than 0, ensuring an all-negative array still returns a correct (negative) answer.

blocks.text: Every possible subarray sum is checked directly via its running sum, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the n starting positions walks forward up to n elements.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: restarting the running sum from scratch at every new starting position ignores that the best subarray ending at any position only ever depends on the best subarray ending at the immediately preceding position, which can be tracked incrementally instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts its running sum from scratch at every starting position. Instead, maintain a single running value: the best subarray sum ending exactly at the current position. At each step, this value either extends the previous one (adding the current element) or discards it and restarts fresh at the current element alone, whichever is larger. Track the overall best value seen across the whole pass.

Maintain current, the best subarray sum ending at the current position, and best, the best subarray sum seen anywhere so far. At each step, update current to max(nums[i], current + nums[i]), then update best to max(best, current).
Track a single running "best ending here" value, restarting it whenever continuing would only hurt.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with O(1) work per element.
Space: O(1) extra.

current always represents the best possible subarray sum that ends exactly at the current position. Since any subarray ending here either includes the element just before it or doesn't, the only two candidates worth comparing are "extend the previous best" and "start fresh here", and taking the larger of the two is always correct. best simply tracks the overall maximum across every position's current value, since the true answer could end anywhere.

items: current and best are both initialized to nums[0], correctly handling arrays that are entirely negative.
The single max(nums[i], current + nums[i]) expression captures the entire "extend or restart" decision in one line.
best is updated every iteration, since the globally best subarray could end at any position, not just the last one.

blocks.text: Kadane's Algorithm rests on the observation that the best subarray ending at any position depends only on the best subarray ending at the position just before it, never on anything further back, collapsing an apparently O(n squared) search into a single linear pass.

items: Initializing best (or current) to 0 instead of nums[0], which breaks on all-negative arrays by incorrectly allowing an "empty subarray" of sum 0 to win.

Comparing current + nums[i] against 0 instead of against nums[i] alone to decide whether to restart, which is a subtly different (and less standard) formulation that still needs the same careful all-negative handling.
Forgetting to update best on every iteration, and only checking it at the very end, which misses cases where the true maximum subarray ends earlier than the last position.

items: State the core recurrence (extend vs. restart) explicitly and explain WHY a negative running sum is always safe to discard, since this justification is exactly what separates a memorized answer from genuine understanding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximum sum of a contiguous subarray" is the canonical signal for Kadane's Algorithm: track a running "best ending here" value, discarding it whenever it goes negative.

items: How would you also report the actual subarray, not just its sum? Track a tentative start index, resetting it whenever a restart happens, and record the (start, end) pair whenever best is updated.

How would this change if the array were circular (the end wraps to the start)? This becomes Maximum Sum Circular Subarray, requiring an additional case analysis comparing the standard Kadane's result against total-sum-minus-minimum-subarray-sum.
What if you needed the maximum sum using at most k elements? This becomes a different sliding-window or prefix-sum-based problem, since Kadane's recurrence alone doesn't track subarray length.

The foundational technique for this entire category; nearly every other Kadane's Algorithm problem (Maximum Absolute Sum, Longest Turbulent Subarray, Maximum Sum Circular Subarray) is a variation of this same "track the best value ending here, decide whether to extend or restart" recurrence.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (Kadane's Algorithm): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Kadane's Algorithm: a single running "best subarray sum ending here" value
Core Idea: At each position, either extend the previous running sum or restart fresh, whichever is larger; a negative running sum is never worth carrying forward
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The best subarray ending at any position depends only on the best subarray ending at the position just before it
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]); best = max(best, current)
